variants.note: an alternative singular form, used for one person of unstated sex; less common than themselves in this use

pronunciation.notes: The stress falls on the second part: *them-SELVES*.

core_idea: **Themselves** refers back to the people or things already meant by **they**, either as the object of their own action or to show that they, no one else, did it.

senses.definition: used as the object of a verb or preposition when the action affects the same people or things that are the subject
senses.explanation: **Themselves** is used when the subject and the object of the same clause refer to the same people: *they blamed themselves*. For one person of unstated sex, **themselves** (or the newer **themself**) is used the same way: *everyone should look after themselves*.

examples.text: They blamed themselves for the delay.
The children taught themselves to swim.
Everyone should be proud of themselves today.
Ask each guest to introduce themselves.

senses.definition: used after a noun or pronoun, or at the end of a clause, to give special attention to the people or things just mentioned, often to show that they did something without help
senses.explanation: This emphatic use often comes right after the subject or at the end of the clause: *they themselves don't believe it*; *they painted the house themselves*.

examples.text: They themselves don't believe the plan will work.
The students organized the trip themselves.

phrases.definition: alone, without other people, or without help

examples.text: The kids played by themselves all afternoon.
They finished the project by themselves.

usage_note: **Themselves** is used only when the subject and the object of the same clause are the same people; it is not a more polite or formal way of saying **them**.

learner_errors.incorrect: We invited themselves to the party.
learner_errors.correct: We invited them to the party.
learner_errors.note: **Themselves** is used only when the subject and the object are the same people; here the subject is **we**, so the plain object form **them** is needed.

adaptation.grammar: English marks a reflexive pronoun with its own form (**myself**, **ourselves**, **themselves**, and so on), different from the ordinary object pronoun; many languages use one reflexive form for every person, or reuse the ordinary object pronoun instead.

provenance.notes: pronunciation.british: the model panel disagrees with the drafter's full-vowel first syllable ðemˈselvz, likely favoring a reduced schwa form; no open data covers British to settle it, so the drafter's transcription is kept meanwhile (reviews/needs_curator.txt).
